e-9560.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Parametric Form
e-9560.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
e-9560.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = 4\cos t, \qquad
	y = 4\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-16(2\pi -0) \\  & =-32\pi \end{aligned}
$$

e-9561.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form
e-9561.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $9x^2 + y^2 = 9.$
e-9561.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{1}10{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

e-9574.knowledge_point: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Non-Closed Curve
e-9574.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/6eebbc5ae9f548f5b00de9a12d454fa788884bf73ad46a1065eab0d26330a921.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
e-9574.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The curve is counterclockwise, so outward flux is ∮(P dy − Q dx). With P=49cos²(t), Q=1, dy=2cos(t)dt, and dx=−7sin(t)dt, the flux is ∫₀²π[98cos³(t)+7sin(t)]dt=0, since both terms integrate to zero over a full period.

after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

Along the curve C, we have x=7cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=x2=49cos2⁡t,Q(x,y)=1.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(7cos⁡t)=−7sin⁡t,dydt=ddt(2sin⁡t)=2cos⁡t.

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution sin⁡t=u,du=cos⁡tdt, as follows:

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∫02π(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫02π(49cos2⁡t)⋅(2cos⁡t)−(1)⋅(−7sin⁡t)dt=∫02π98cos3⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98cos2⁡t⋅cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98(1−sin2⁡t)cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98(cos⁡t−sin2⁡tcos⁡t)+7sin⁡tdt=∫02π98cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt+∫02π−98sin2⁡tcos⁡tdt=∫02π98cos⁡t+7sin⁡tdt+∫00−98u2du=(98sin⁡t−7cos⁡t)|02π+0=0

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={x}^{2}\,i+j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=49{cos}^{2}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=u,du=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(49{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(1)\cdot (-7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{3}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-98{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }98\operatorname{cos}⁡t+7\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{0}-98{u}^{2}\,du \\  & =(98\operatorname{sin}⁡t-7\operatorname{cos}⁡t){|}_{0}^{2\pi }+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$

$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=xy\,i+{x}^{2}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+8\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{1}-16{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}

$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+y\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =30{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }1\,\text{d}t \\  & =30(2\pi -0) \\  & =60\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4x=4(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=32\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =4y=4(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(32\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(24\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }192\,\text{d}t \\  & =192t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =192(2\pi -0) \\  & =384\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =9{x}^{3}=9{cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=u,du=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(9{cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{1}^{1}(u+{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=y\,i+9{x}^{3}\,j$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =9{x}^{3}=9{cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $\operatorname{cos}⁡t=u,du=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(9{cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{1}^{1}(u+{u}^{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $1,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.

\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x-16y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t-16\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =x+y=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

decision.explanation: The ellipse is x²/16+y²/4=1, so use x=4cos(t), y=2sin(t) counterclockwise. Outward flux is ∮(3x dy−3y dx)=∫₀²π24[cos²(t)+sin²(t)]dt=48π.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3x\,i+3y\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=3x\,i+3y\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3x=12\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =3y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24{cos}^{2}⁡t+24{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }24\,\text{d}t \\  & =24t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =24(2\pi -0) \\  & =48\pi \end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{3}\,i+{x}^{3}\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={1}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{3}={sin}^{3}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{3}={cos}^{3}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({sin}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{3}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({sin}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=(y-x)\,i-(x+y)\,j$ across the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={3}^{2}.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is a circle centered at the origin with the radius $1.$ It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }-({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}t \\  & =-9t\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-9(2\pi -0) \\  & =-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=x\,i+{y}^{2}\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/d432857e3350dfcb70a2a00b66ad9b86bc207382edd277c2169be0834c1710e0.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{t},\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =x=\frac{1}{t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(\frac{1}{t})\cdot (1)-({t}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}\frac{1}{t}+1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡2+2)-(\operatorname{ln}⁡\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is given by $y=1-x$ from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=1-t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/e288ed1095be61e4645fb63c22b7fd2cb605d34795c30557e84afb31b7ec8721.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1)\cdot (-1)-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2-0 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/cd21413d8eea5e2fec67eebe22967c846fd7916fd4fb0fbe5f8efe7ac9df6b1a.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y=1-x$ from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=\,i+\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=1-t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(1,0).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/e288ed1095be61e4645fb63c22b7fd2cb605d34795c30557e84afb31b7ec8721.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =1, \\ Q(x,y) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1)\cdot (-1)-(1)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-2t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-2-0 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,y=t,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(1,2.)$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/b7ac1ce4a79528f5660b8f898739da72489ebe8e8fc156020efae77a103fbec4.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2, \\ Q(x,y) & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2)\cdot (1)-(-4)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2+2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2t+{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(2\cdot 2+{2}^{2})-0 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

If F=Pi+Qj is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of F across C measured with respect to a unit normal vector n on C is given by ∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx. To apply this formula,

  • the curve should be parameterized as r(t) for t∈[a,b], and

  • the unit normal vector n must be a 90∘ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector T(t).

In this case, n is indeed a 90∘ clockwise rotation of T, so we can apply the above formula.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2,y=12t.

Therefore,

P(x,y)=4,Q(x,y)=2.

Computing the derivatives of x(t) and y(t) along the curve, we get

dxdt=ddt(t2)=12,dydt=ddt(12t)=−12t2.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∫CF⋅nds=∫CPdy−Qdx=∫1/22(P⋅dydt−Q⋅dxdt)dt=∫1/22(4)⋅(−12t2)−(2)⋅(12)dt=∫1/22−2t2−1dt=(2t−t)|1/22=(1−2)−(4−12)=−92

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/414611a90c2227ff163d40a4f6f560bc67c471fa0f35724e459cec280e4904f9.png)

Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=4\,i+2\,j$ through the curve $C$ given by $r(t)=\frac{t}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2t}\,j$ for $t\in [\frac{1}{2},2],$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
content.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/11376e6ef18b151a6dd1a02dd09f20b72bce3160c718f4095b4f08b23721ff1f.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=\frac{t}{2},\,y=\frac{1}{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =4, \\ Q(x,y) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{2})=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2t})=-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(4)\cdot (-\frac{1}{2{t}^{2}})-(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{2}{t}-t){|}_{1/2}^{2} \\  & =(1-2)-(4-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

In this case, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062142/assets/0e751adb9f44d24ba89af318fe5f063b1be146bbae45d05fc2dd9a99bef259f2.png)

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =3xy=3{t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =2x+1=2t+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{2})(1)-(2t+1)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}-2t-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-1-1)-(0-0-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{2})(1)-(2t+1)(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}-2t-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{3}-{t}^{2}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(1-1-1)-(0-0-0) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$
